cells.tense: You are in the middle of it, and you have the words for it.
cells.ask: Write down the sentence you would say the next time something tips, before it happens, and keep it where you'll see it.
cells.core:
You're the one who notices when something has gone off between people, and instead of sitting on it you put words to it. Not a hammer, not a diplomat. You say the thing that's true at the size it actually is, which is why people bring you the difficult stuff.
That runs quietly, and keeping it running costs something. Somebody has to know when to speak and when not to, and in that moment it's you. So today isn't about getting better at it. It's about making one of those sentences visible, so this has a floor under it. Put the next one down somewhere you'll see it, in your own words, before the moment comes. Keeping things level doesn't need defending. It needs one record of itself.
cells.sheetLine: You keep things level, and you know how it's done.
cells.verb: Holding perception clear and saying what is true at the size it actually is.
cells.place: Where the scale gets leveled again after it has tipped.

cells.tense: You're correcting things before they've had a chance to go wrong.
cells.ask: Pick one situation this week and say nothing in it, even when you see the fix, and notice what happens on its own.
cells.core:
You've started running the correction ahead of the event. Before someone has said the unfair thing, you've already prepared the answer. Before the meeting has tipped, you've pre-balanced it in your head, and by the time you speak you're not talking to what's here — you're talking to the version you braced for.
This is the same gift, spending itself in advance. The eye stays sharp, but the room stops reaching you, because you're not in it yet. Fairness isn't something you imitate ahead of time; it's what shows up when you're actually in contact. Let one thing go without your hand on it, and find out from inside the moment whether it holds.

cells.tense: The words for what's off are still in you, and they're not coming out.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true thing about how something landed for you this week, without softening it or cleaning it up first.
cells.core:
You can see what's off. You clock the imbalance, you know who's carrying more, you know what sentence would set it right. What stopped is the saying.
The plain version doesn't leave your mouth anymore, and the eye just registers and moves on. So the fairness has no hand in the world. You watch the scale tip and you eat the difference. That's not the same as not caring. It's caring with nowhere to go.
Start smaller than being braver. Tell one person one true thing about how a situation landed for you, the plain version, this week. The energy to say more comes from there, not from pushing yourself into it.

cells.tense: The room is already being leveled by you, and the story says it just happened that way.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, about one thing you quietly evened out this week: that was you, you did that.
cells.core:
In how you take your turn in the conversation, how you stop the pile-on, how you bring the quieter person back in — that's the balance running, and it's shaping what's available to the people in the room.
But when you describe it, it comes out as the way things are, or that's just how it went. The work is there. The claim isn't. So it doesn't count toward anything, and nobody gets to see it for what it is, including you.
You don't have to do more of it. Take one thing you evened out this week — a moment you brought something back into proportion and called it nothing — and say out loud, once, that it was you who did that.

attempts.check: The record hands me a card about being the steady one for what's true, seated in fairness, but the cell that has to work is the person's relationship with their own calibration, which this seat names only at the level of a general description; it does not tell me whether the person is the one who over-corrects or the one who under-asserts. The reader could reasonably say: no, my problem isn't with keeping things fair, it's with what I can't get done. If I'm wrong about the card, the ask still survives, because giving someone the next sentence when the imbalance appears to them is useful whether or not they accept this card. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'You've been the one who keeps the thing true,' which is a compliment I might enjoy giving more than they need to hear it — cut it down to the visible act.
